gaps.description: $M dollar directive for macro file path in .pmlmac header — KB lists $M in dollar-command table but provides no example of $M as a macro header declaration.
object BLOCK(...) constructor syntax for evaluate() — KB documents Evaluate(BLOCK command) method but never shows the object BLOCK(...) constructor form.
.:  attribute access syntax from DBREF — KB shows DBREF examples via .query() and .qreal() but does not document the .:  notation for direct PDMS object attribute access.
$! variable substitution inside $P print command — KB mentions $! as a substitution symbol but lacks examples in macro print contexts.
eqnocase() method for case-insensitive comparison — KB documents .eq() but does not cover .eqnocase() for case-insensitive string comparison.

DBREF-to-PDMS-attribute navigation via .:  — no KB pattern covers using !!ce as a DBREF context then accessing PDMS-specific attributes like HavePartTerminals, refPropagatedSignals, HavePartOutGoingConnections via .:  syntax.
collectallfor with empty condition || for world-wide collection — KB has collectallfor examples but not the empty-condition world-scope pattern.
Nested DO/ENDDO with indices iteration and conditional collection.remove() — KB has simple DO/ENDDO examples but not nested index-based iteration with in-place collection mutation.
No HANDLE/ENDHANDLE error wrapping in either original or benchmark — PDMS macro operations on DBREFs should be wrapped in error handlers to gracefully handle missing elements.
No UNDOABLE transaction wrapping — modifying PDMS object attributes (HavePartOutGoingConnections, HavePartIncomingConnections) should be wrapped in an undoable block.

Inconsistent attribute casing in original: HavePartTerminals vs havepartchannelTerminals vs Havepartoutgoingconnections vs HavePartOutGoingConnections vs HavePartChannelTerminals vs HavePartOutGoingConnections vs HavePartIncomingConnections. No KB entry documents canonical AVEVA PDMS attribute names.
!outConn[1] accessed after !outConn.remove(1) — the first element is removed then the (now-second) element at index 1 is accessed without checking if the array still has elements.
!markings.findFirst(!marking) result !i used as index without checking !i > 0 — findFirst returns 0 if not found, which would cause an invalid index access.
break statement in inner loop stops processing ALL remaining incoming connections — semantically questionable for a terminal-correction macro.

Double assignment: !terminal.:HavePartOutGoingConnections = !outConn reassigns the original array reference after removing element 1, potentially causing inconsistency with !tempOutConn already removed.
PDMS-specific attributes refPropagatedSignals, HavePartOutGoingConnections, HavePartIncomingConnections, HavePartChannelTerminals, RefConnectionsOut, RefConnectionsIn are not documented in KB.
RefConnectionsOut.acttype returning :IncomingConnection string — no KB entry covers connection type enumeration.
Macro depends on running PDMS session with CE elements loaded — no KB entry documents macro runtime prerequisites for PDMS-dependent macros.

newEntriesNeeded.title: DBREF-to-PDMS-Object Attribute Access via .:  Syntax
newEntriesNeeded.principle: Use .:  (dot-colon) notation to access PDMS object attributes from a PML DBREF variable. Unlike .query() which returns attribute values as strings, .:  provides direct object reference access for nested attribute chains.
newEntriesNeeded.rule: After assigning a DBREF to a PML variable, use !dbref.:AttributeName to access any PDMS object attribute. Nested attributes chain with additional .: , e.g., !obj.:HavePartOutGoingConnections.[1].:RefConnectionsOut.
newEntriesNeeded.exampleCanonical:
-- CB mac_46
!ces = !!collectallfor(|CE|, ||, world)
do !ce values !ces
  !!ce = !ce
  !terminals = !!ce.:HavePartTerminals
  !outConn   = !terminal.:HavePartOutGoingConnections
enddo
newEntriesNeeded.exampleAntipattern:
-- BAD: Using .query() for nested attributes
!attr = !ce.query(|HavePartOutGoingConnections|)
-- .query() returns a string, not a collection reference
pitfalls: .:  requires a valid PDMS object reference; a BADREF will throw an error
Unlike .query(), .:  returns the actual object/collection, not a string value
Attribute names are case-insensitive in PML but should follow AVEVA canonical casing
newEntriesNeeded.sourcedoc: AVEVA PDMS Customization Guide — Object Attribute Access

newEntriesNeeded.title: object BLOCK(...) Constructor for Collection Evaluation
newEntriesNeeded.principle: Use object BLOCK(...) to create an inline code block that can be passed to collection methods like evaluate(). The block is evaluated once per collection element with the element referenced by the loop variable.
newEntriesNeeded.rule: Wrap a PML expression in object BLOCK(|expression|) to pass it as a block argument. Inside the block, use the loop variable name (e.g., !evalIndex) to access the current collection element.
newEntriesNeeded.exampleAntipattern:
-- BAD: Passing a string instead of a block
!markings = !channelTerminals.evaluate('|!channelTerminals[!evalIndex].:marking[1]|')
pitfalls: The variable name inside object BLOCK must match the implicit iteration variable of the collection
object BLOCK(...) is not the same as a string expression — it creates a PML code block
Block variables are scoped to the evaluate() call

newEntriesNeeded.title: Canonical AVEVA PDMS Terminal and Connection Attribute Names
newEntriesNeeded.principle: PDMS objects use specific PascalCased attribute names for terminal and connection management. These attributes are case-insensitive in PML but should be referenced with canonical casing for consistency.
newEntriesNeeded.rule: Use the canonical attribute names listed below when accessing terminal and connection data on PDMS objects. Do not mix casing within a single codebase.
newEntriesNeeded.exampleAntipattern:
-- BAD: Inconsistent casing in same file
!terminals = !!ce.:HavePartTerminals
!chanTerms = !channel.:havepartchannelTerminals  -- should be HavePartChannelTerminals
!outConn   = !terminal.:Havepartoutgoingconnections  -- should be HavePartOutGoingConnections
pitfalls: Attribute names are case-insensitive in PML but inconsistent casing causes maintenance issues
Some attributes return collections (ARRAY/COLLECTION), others return single values
refPropagatedSignals may be unset() for terminals with no propagated signals
newEntriesNeeded.sourcedoc: AVEVA PDMS Object Reference — Terminal and Connection Attributes

newEntriesNeeded.title: Case-Insensitive String Comparison with eqnocase()
newEntriesNeeded.principle: Use .eqnocase() method for case-insensitive string comparison. This is equivalent to .eq() but ignores letter case differences.
newEntriesNeeded.rule: Call .eqnocase(|value|) on a STRING object to compare against another string ignoring case. Returns TRUE if strings match regardless of case.
newEntriesNeeded.exampleAntipattern:
-- BAD: Using .eq() for case-insensitive comparison
!isMatch = !str1.eq(|:incomingconnection|)  -- fails if case differs
pitfalls: eqnocase() is a STRING method; ensure the receiver is a STRING
Not available on non-string PML types
Use .eq() for case-sensitive comparison when needed

newEntriesNeeded.title: Nested DO/ENDDO with Indices Iteration and Collection.remove()
newEntriesNeeded.principle: When iterating over a collection by indices and conditionally removing elements, the loop index must account for shifting indices after removal. Using 'indices' in the DO clause captures the index set at loop entry time, but removing elements shifts subsequent indices.
newEntriesNeeded.rule: When using DO !idx indices !collection with conditional .remove(), be aware that removing element at !idx shifts all higher indices down by 1. Consider iterating in reverse or using a while loop with manual index control.
newEntriesNeeded.syntax:
do !idx indices !collection
  !ele = !collection[!idx]
  if (shouldRemove(!ele)) then
    !collection.remove(!idx)
    -- Note: higher indices have shifted!
  endif
enddo
newEntriesNeeded.exampleCanonical:
-- CB mac_46
do !d indices !incConn
  !ele = !incConn[!d]
  if (!refCon.unset()) then
    !incConn.remove(!d)
  else
    break
  endif
enddo
newEntriesNeeded.exampleAntipattern:
-- BAD: Assuming indices are stable after remove
-- This loop may skip elements or access invalid indices
pitfalls: remove() shifts all higher indices — elements may be skipped
Using 'indices' captures the index set at loop start; removed elements still have valid index values but point to different elements
break exits the entire loop, potentially leaving unprocessed elements
